block.heading: A minimum price on a diagram
block.text:
With mahangu at an equilibrium of N$200 and 300 bags a week, a minimum price of N$250 raises quantity supplied to 400 but cuts quantity demanded to 200: farmers offer 400 bags but sell 200, a surplus of 200.

![Minimum price on mahangu](diagrams/item-6145-6.3-018-proc-answer.png)

item.prompt: Farmers supply 200, 300, 400 and 500 bags of mahangu (pearl millet) a week at N$150, N$200, N$250 and N$300 a bag, and buyers demand 400, 300, 200 and 100 bags at those prices, as in the diagram. To protect farmers' incomes, the government sets a minimum price of N$250 a bag. Use the diagram to show the original equilibrium, the minimum price and its effect on the market (4).
item.canonical_answer: The original equilibrium E, where D meets S, is N$200 a bag and 300 bags a week. Draw the minimum price as a horizontal line at N$250, above the equilibrium price, so it is binding. Neither curve shifts: at N$250 quantity supplied, read off S, is 400 bags and quantity demanded, read off D, is 200 bags. Supply exceeds demand, so there is a surplus of 200 bags a week. Farmers offer 400 bags but only 200 are bought, fewer than the 300 sold before; the surplus stays unsold unless the government or another buyer purchases it.
